newsitem.title: USA: High Texas boll count boosted US cotton total - USDA.
newsitem.headline: High Texas boll count boosted US cotton total - USDA.

text.p: A record boll count in Texas was a factor in pushing the Lone Star state to a record cotton yield and lifting the U.S. crop to the second highest total ever, a U.S. Agriculture Department official said Thursday.
USDA's January crop report pegged the U.S. cotton crop at 18.95 million bales with an average yield of 709 lbs per acre.

Texas had an Upland cotton yield of 522 lbs per acre, aided by its highest boll count ever and its second highest boll weight, said Ray Halley, chief of the crops branch of the National Agricultural Statistics Service at USDA. Thirty percent of Texas cotton acreage was abandoned.
"It's considerably above what their normal abandonment is," Halley told reporters after the crop report was released.

About 12.5 percent of U.S. cotton acreage was abandoned. The figure usually is three to five percent, Halley said. The upsurge for the 1996 crop was due to dry spring weather and summer hurricane damage.
Good weather in the late summer and fall gave the Texas crop a boost.
While Texas and Georgia notched sizable increases from USDA's December estimates, South Carolina, Mississippi and Florida saw losses in estimated output.
As of January 1, 17.68 million bales of cotton had been ginned from the current crop, compared to 17.01 at this point a year ago.

Halley said the larger ginning figure indicated good harvesting weather and that gins were getting more cotton earlier. Some cotton remains to be picked in Texas, he said, where gins might be open until early February.
